methods.label: Subtract the four corner gaps
methods.explanation:
The hexagons overlap, so an enclosing square provides a useful way to calculate the area: subtract the four congruent corner gaps from that square.

[Figure 1](figures/2022_AMC_12B_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

Use the orientation shown in the figure. Each hexagon extends across the central square; for example, the hexagon sharing its bottom edge extends upward. All hexagon sides have length \(1\), because their shared edges are sides of the unit square.

Write \(s=\sqrt3\). Dividing a unit-sided regular hexagon into six equilateral triangles shows that the distance between opposite parallel sides is \(s\). Indeed, each equilateral triangle has altitude
\[
\sqrt{1-(1/2)^2}=\frac{s}{2}.
\]
The upward-extending hexagon therefore reaches \(s-1\) above the central square. The corresponding extensions in the other three directions are equal. The remaining hexagon vertices stay within these four extreme lines: their sideways overhang is only \(1/2<s-1\). Hence the enclosing square has side length
\[
L=1+2(s-1)=2s-1.
\]

Consider its upper-right corner \(C\). Let \(A\) be the right endpoint of the polygon's top horizontal side, and let \(B\) be the upper endpoint of its right vertical side. Those straight sides each have length \(1\) and are centered on the enclosing square's sides, so
\[
CA=CB=\frac{L-1}{2}=s-1.
\]
Let \(Q\) be the inward vertex where the two sloping boundary edges from \(A\) and \(B\) meet. The corner gap is the quadrilateral \(CAQB\). These four corner gaps are the entire omitted region: the hexagons cover the horizontal and vertical strips through the central square, while adjacent hexagons provide the two boundary edges in each remaining corner.

Reflection across the diagonal through \(C\) interchanges the adjacent hexagons and fixes \(Q\). Thus \(Q\) has equal perpendicular distances from the top and right sides of the enclosing square. Call this distance \(x\), and let \(F\) be the perpendicular foot from \(Q\) to \(CA\). The diagonal symmetry gives \(CF=QF=x\), so
\[
AF=s-1-x.
\]
The hexagon edge \(AQ\) makes a \(60^\circ\) angle with the horizontal. The legs of the right triangle \(AFQ\) therefore have ratio \(1:s\), giving
\[
x=s(s-1-x).
\]
Solving,
\[
x=\frac{s(s-1)}{1+s}=2s-3.
\]
Here \(3/2<s<2\), so \(x>0\) and \(AF=2-s\) lies between \(0\) and \(1/2\), consistent with the intersection lying on the indicated hexagon edges.

Split the gap along \(CQ\). The two triangles have bases \(CA=CB=s-1\) and corresponding heights \(x\). Their combined area is
\[
(s-1)x=(s-1)(2s-3).
\]
Subtracting all four gaps, the polygon's area is
\[
\begin{aligned}
L^2-4(s-1)(2s-3)
&=(2s-1)^2-4(s-1)(2s-3)\\
&=16s-23\\
&=16\sqrt3-23.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(3\) is squarefree, \(m=16\), \(n=3\), and \(p=-23\). Therefore
\[
m+n+p=16+3-23=\boxed{-4},
\]
choice \(\boxed{B}\).

review.mathematicalCheck: The figure confirms the overlapping hexagons extend across the square as stated. Their opposite-side distance is √3, giving enclosing side 2√3-1. Diagonal symmetry and the 60-degree boundary edge give x=√3(√3-1-x)=2√3-3. The intersection lies on the actual edges. The four corner gaps exhaust the omitted region, each with area (√3-1)(2√3-3). Subtraction yields 16√3-23, so m+n+p=-4.
